summary: Defines carrying V5.2 messages over IP using SCTP between a Signaling Gateway and a Media Gateway Controller. It builds on the ISDN User Adaptation Layer and updates RFC 3057.

plainLanguage.summary: Old telephone exchange signals can be packed into internet messages. This explains how to carry them across.

questions: what is v5.2 backhaul over sctp
what is an envelope function address
subtitle: How a gateway carries old V5.2 telephone-exchange signaling over IP, by extending the ISDN adaptation layer.

tldr.problem: A V5.2 interface links a local telephone exchange to an access network over E1 lines, and its signaling has to be carried over IP between a Signaling Gateway and a Media Gateway Controller.
tldr.mechanism: V5UA extends the ISDN User Adaptation Layer (IUA) from RFC 3057 and runs over SCTP. It adds an Envelope Function Address to the message header, a naming scheme for links and channels, and new messages for link status, Sa-bit handling and overload.
tldr.outcome: V5.2 signaling can be backhauled over IP while the layer 1 state machine stays on the gateway and system management sits on the controller. The RFC updates RFC 3057.

today: RFC 3807 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 3057, the ISDN User Adaptation Layer.

sections.title: Backhauling V5.2 over IP
sections.content:
RFC 3807 describes how to carry V5.2 messages over IP using SCTP. The two ends are a Signaling Gateway (SG), which receives V5.2 signaling over a standard V5.2 interface, and a Media Gateway Controller (MGC). V5.2 is an ETSI interface between a Local Exchange (LE) and an Access Network (AN). It covers analog telephone access, ISDN basic rate access and ISDN primary rate access.

V5UA is an extension of the ISDN User Adaptation Layer (IUA, RFC 3057). Everything defined in IUA is also valid for V5UA unless this document says otherwise. The RFC does not describe V5 itself, which is defined by ETSI standards. It only explains enough of V5 to make the text understandable.

IUA is not enough on its own because V5.2 layer 2, and especially layer 3, differs from the Q.921 and Q.931 layers that IUA adapts.
sections.plainLanguage: V5UA is a way to ship old phone-exchange messages across the internet. It borrows most of its rules from an earlier system for ISDN and adds the extras V5.2 needs.

sections.title: V5.2 Basics
sections.content:
A V5.2 interface joins the LE and the AN with up to 16 E1 (PCM30) links of 2048 kbit/s each. Unlike V5.1, which uses links without concentration, V5.2 supports concentration. Time slots 16, 15 and 31 on any E1 link can be reserved for data communication between LE and AN. These are the communication channels (C-channels), and a logical path for one protocol over them is a C-path.

V5.2 uses a bearer channel connection protocol to set up bearer connections on demand, a link control protocol for multi-link management, and a protection protocol for switching channels when links fail. Layer 2 is LAPV5-EF and LAPV5-DL. Layer 3 is V5-Link Control, V5-BCC, V5-PSTN, V5-Control and V5-Protection.

An Envelope Function Address (EFA) is a 13-bit number from 0 to 8191. It identifies one of the five V5.2 protocols or an ISDN agent on the AN.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a bundle of up to 16 cables, with a few lanes on each cable set aside for control chatter. Each kind of chatter has its own label so it reaches the right listener.

sections.title: Splitting the Work Between SG and MGC
sections.content:
The V5 protocol entities are split across the two boxes. The SG holds LAPV5-DL and LAPV5-EF, facing the AN. The MGC holds Link Control, Control, BCC, PSTN and Protection. V5 System Management SHALL be on the MGC, the V5 Layer 1 Functional State Machine (L1 FSM) SHALL be on the SG, and Dynamic TEI Management for V5 BRI SHALL be on the MGC.

The client/server model follows IUA. The registered port for V5UA, for SCTP and also UDP and TCP, is 5675.

On SCTP streams, the RFC says a single stream SHOULD carry BCC, Link Control, Control and PSTN for one C-channel, a separate stream SHOULD carry Protection, and one stream SHOULD carry all ISDN user ports on that C-channel. One stream SHOULD NOT carry more than one C-channel. A separate stream SHOULD carry all MPH (link related) messages.
sections.plainLanguage: One box listens to the phone line and handles the low-level conversation. The other box is the manager that makes the decisions. They talk over the internet, with separate lanes for different kinds of talk.

sections.title: Message Header and Interface Identifier
sections.content:
V5UA changes the IUA message header by putting the EFA into the field that IUA left as Spare. The DLCI tag changes from 0x5 to 0x81. For MPH messages that do not use DLCI and EFA, SAPI, TEI and EFA SHALL be set to zero and ignored by the receiver.

IUA names C-channels without tying them to a link, which V5 cannot accept, so V5UA requires a naming convention. The integer Interface Identifier is split into a 27-bit Link Identifier, which MUST be unique on the SG, and a 5-bit Chnl ID. The Chnl ID is the time slot number, so valid values are 15, 16 and 31. For link management messages it MUST be 0. A text-formatted identifier is the hex representation of the integer, written as a variable length string.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message gets an address label saying which cable and which lane it belongs to, plus a note about what kind of conversation it is part of.

sections.title: New Message Types
sections.content:
V5 boundary primitives get a new message class, 14, called V5 Boundary Primitives Transport Messages (V5PTM). The classes IUA already uses stay valid: 0 for Management, 3 for ASP State Maintenance and 4 for ASP Traffic Maintenance. Message types 1 to 10 reuse the Q.921/Q.931 data, unit data, establish and release messages. Types 11 to 18 are new.

Link Status messages (types 11, 12, 13) let System Management on the MGC track the state of each E1 link, whether or not it carries C-channels. Link Status Indication carries a Link Status parameter (tag 0x82) with value 0x0 for operational or 0x1 for non-operational.

Sa-Bit messages (types 14 to 17) set and read the Sa7 bit used by the Link Identification procedure. Their parameter (tag 0x83) holds a BIT ID, where only Sa7 (0x7) is valid, and a Bit Value of 0x0 or 0x1. The Sa7 bit is ONE in normal operation and ZERO during link identification.

The Error Indication message (type 18, tag 0x84) has one valid reason, OVERLOAD (0x1).
sections.plainLanguage: V5UA adds a few new kinds of notes: one that says whether a cable works, one for flipping a small flag on the cable, and one that shouts when a lane is too busy.

sections.title: Link Status, Failure and Overload Procedures
sections.content:
V5 System Management SHALL send Link Status Start Reporting for all links on an interface when it is activated. The SG SHALL answer immediately with a Link Status Indication and then send one on every change. If the link is already active, the SG reports its current status at once. Stop Reporting SHALL be sent for all links on interface deactivation. The SG must not reply, assumes the link is out of service and SHALL take L2 down on that link.

On a layer 1 failure, V5 Layer 2 is notified directly by V5 Layer 1 on the SG, and the SG sends Link Status Indication with NON-OPERATIONAL. System management SHALL NOT send an MPH-Layer_1 Failure Ind to Layer 2 in response.

If SCTP failure or loss of heartbeat is detected, the ASP acts as if it received a non-operational Link Status Indication for every link on that SG. It SHALL keep trying to reconnect, and on success sends Link Status Start Reporting for all links on active V5 interfaces.

If the SG cannot process all Layer 3 messages on a C-channel in time, it SHOULD send an Error Indication with reason Overload. It SHALL resend while the overload lasts, and 120 seconds is the RECOMMENDED interval.
sections.plainLanguage: The manager asks the line box to report whether each cable works and to keep reporting changes. If the connection drops, the manager assumes every cable is down until it hears otherwise.

sections.title: Example: Link Identification
sections.content:
The RFC gives two message flows for the V5.2 Link Identification procedure, one started by the LE and one started by the AN. In both, the association between ASP and SG is already up and the V5 interface is in service. The procedure itself is defined by the V5.2 standard.

In the LE-initiated flow, Link Control messages (FE-IDReq, FE-IDAck, FE-IDRel) travel as Data Request and Data Indication messages. The ASP uses an Sa-Bit Status Request for Sa7 and the SG reports ZERO. In the AN-initiated flow, the ASP uses Sa-Bit Set Req to set Sa7 to ZERO and later back to ONE, and the SG confirms each time.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like checking you are holding the right end of the right cable: both sides pass notes and flip a small flag on the cable to prove it.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security considerations of the SIGTRAN security document, RFC 3788, apply to this document. The RFC adds nothing of its own.

IANA registered SCTP payload protocol identifier 6 for V5UA. It SHOULD be included in each SCTP DATA chunk. The value 0 (unspecified) is also allowed, and any other value MUST NOT be used. IANA also registered port 5675 for V5UA.
sections.plainLanguage: V5UA borrows its safety rules from a shared rulebook for this family of protocols, and it was given its own number and port so traffic can be recognized.
